Profitable
PROF-it-uh-bl
adj.
From Latin proficere, to advance or make progress. Webster 1828: yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; useful; advantageous. Paul uses it of Scripture, of godliness, and of a runaway slave who had become useful — a pun on Onesimus’ own name.

Biblical Definition

Profitable is the adjective Paul attaches to the two things that actually repay a man’s investment. The first is Scripture: All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness: That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works (2 Timothy 3:16-17). The four uses are a complete pastoral toolkit — what to believe, what is wrong, how to be set right, and how to be trained in a right course — and the stated end is a man thoroughly equipped. The second is godliness: bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come (1 Timothy 4:8). Paul is not disparaging the body; he is comparing returns, and the return on godliness runs into the next world. The third use is personal and gently humorous. Onesimus, whose name means useful, ran away from Philemon and was converted under Paul’s ministry in prison, and Paul writes: Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me (Philemon 1:11). The gospel does not merely forgive a useless man; it makes him what his name always said.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PROFITABLE as yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; and also useful, advantageous, or improving. The commercial and the moral senses both stand in the entry, as they do in Paul’s usage.

expand to see more

PROFITABLE, a. — Yielding or bringing profit or gain; gainful; lucrative; as a profitable trade.

Useful; advantageous; improving; as a profitable study or discourse.

PROFIT, n. — Gain; advantage; any accession of good from labor or exertion.

The Latin proficere means to go forward, to advance — profit is progress before it is money.

Onesimus, the name of the slave in Philemon, is Greek for useful or profitable, and Paul plays on it in verse 11.

Key Scripture

2 Timothy 3:16 — "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:"

2 Timothy 3:17 — "That the man of God may be perfect, throughly furnished unto all good works."

1 Timothy 4:8 — "For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come."

Philemon 1:11 — "Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me:"

Acts 20:31 — "Therefore watch, and remember, that by the space of three years I ceased not to warn every one night and day with tears."

Modern Corruption

2 Timothy 3:16 is the church’s charter for the sufficiency of Scripture, and it is emptied from two sides — by a criticism that grants inspiration in some diminished sense, and by a piety that reads the Bible for comfort and never for reproof or correction.

expand to see more

All scripture is given by inspiration of God — God-breathed, in one Greek word — and Paul makes no exceptions and grades no portions. Theories that locate inspiration in the reader’s encounter, or in the text’s religious value, or in some kernel within a husk, all founder on the adjective all and on the fact that the Scripture Paul had in view was chiefly the Old Testament, including the genealogies, the ceremonial law, and the histories which modern criticism treats as least profitable. The 1689 Confession begins here, with the Holy Scripture as the only sufficient, certain, and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith, and obedience. Everything else in the confession depends on that first chapter.

The devotional corruption is milder and more widespread. Paul lists four profits and Christians reliably want one: doctrine yes, instruction in righteousness perhaps, but reproof and correction are the two that hurt, and a great deal of modern Bible reading is arranged to avoid them. A verse-a-day of encouragement is not what the apostle described. He describes a book that tells a man he is wrong and then sets him right, and the promised outcome is not a warmed heart but a man throughly furnished unto all good works. The furnishing requires the reproof. And 1 Timothy 4:8 supplies the reason anyone would submit to it: the return on godliness covers this life and the next, which no other investment does.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek ophelimos (G5624), useful, profitable; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed, in the same verse; Onesimos (G3682), profitable, the slave’s name.

expand to see more

Greek ophelimos (G5624) — profitable, useful; 2 Timothy 3:16, 1 Timothy 4:8, Titus 3:8.

Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed, inspired of God; a hapax legomenon at 2 Timothy 3:16.

Greek artios (G739) — fitted, complete; that the man of God may be perfect (2 Timothy 3:17).

Greek exartizo (G1822) — to fit out completely, to equip; throughly furnished unto all good works.

Greek Onesimos (G3682) — Onesimus; profitable, useful — the name Paul puns on in Philemon 11.

Usage

"All scripture… is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction (2 Timothy 3:16) — four profits, and two of them sting."

"Godliness is profitable unto all things (1 Timothy 4:8) — a return that runs into the next world."

"In time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable (Philemon 1:11) — a man made what his name said."
